query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Doping a bulk AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with ~5 at.% Ag will promote the in-situ formation of a ~400 nm thick, adaptive oxide nanocomposite tribolayer during sliding, leading to simultaneous reductions in friction and wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk cast or consolidated AlCoCrFeNi HEA with a homogeneous dual-phase (BCC-based) microstructure, untreated with reactive dopants.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~5 at.% Ag into the alloy during synthesis (e.g., via melting or powder consolidation) to achieve compositional modification.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests in air over a broad temperature range from room temperature (RT) up to approximately 600 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The segregation of Ag during friction leads to nucleation of Ag-containing oxide nanocrystals embedded within an amorphous oxide matrix (~400 nm thick) at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, environmental oxygen reacts with the surface; Ag acts as a catalyst that accelerates the formation of a strong yet deformable oxide nanocomposite layer that reduces direct asperity contact, thereby lowering both the coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy (COF ~0.2 and high wear rate), the Ag-doped alloy is predicted to reduce the COF by approximately 50% (e.g., to around 0.1) and lower wear rates by roughly one order of magnitude.
generation.baseline: Untreated AlCoCrFeNi HEA without Ag exhibits higher friction due to metal-to-metal contact and less-developed protective oxide layers.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness assumes availability of environmental oxygen and operation within the temperature range where Ag segregation and oxide formation are favored (up to ~600 °C).
generation.uncertainty: Long-term durability of the formed tribolayer under cyclic loading and variations in atmospheric humidity remain to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi samples—one with ~5 at.% Ag doping and one without—and conduct ball-on-disk friction tests over RT to 600 °C in ambient air. Use surface characterization (e.g., SEM, TEM, XPS) to detect the formation and structure of the tribolayer.
measurements: Wear scar dimensions and wear rate
Microstructural analysis of the worn surface (e.g., presence and thickness of oxide nanocomposite layer)
Phase identification of segregated Ag and oxide constituents
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-doped samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in COF (i.e., <30% reduction relative to baseline) and do not form a distinct oxide nanocomposite layer compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). Here, we propose an alloy design concept based on an enthalpy-guided approach to promote formation of solid solution nanocrystals, rather than crystalline oxide nanoparticles, in the amorphous matrix during wear. This structure enables a high strength and homogeneous plastic deformation of the friction-induced oxidic nanocomposite surface layer. We realize this concept in a multi-component (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy, by blending a TiNbZr medium-entropy alloy with Ag to create the desired self-lubricating nanostructure upon wear exposure. A ball-on-disk sliding test at a maximum contact stress of 1.0 GPa reveals that the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy exhibits a friction coefficient of around 0.09 in air. The tribological contact introduces environmental O into the alloy, facilitating new atomic coordination with large negative enthalpy of mixing, which enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability. Besides, Ag has a positive enthalpy of mixing with Nb (+16 kJ/mol), which serves as a thermodynamic driving force for the nucleation of Ag nanocrystals from the amorphous matrix. In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals. The high wear resistance of the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy is achieved by the synergistic effect of the low friction coefficient (~0.09) of the alloy and the in-situ formation of an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface, which exhibits a high strength and homogeneous plastic flow behavior. papers.title: Role of Magnesium Perrhenate in an Oil/Solid Mixed System for Tribological Application at Various Temperatures.
papers.system: PAO6 base oil blended with Mg(ReO4)2 additive; tested with a Ni-base superalloy and silicon nitride counterbody
papers.approach: Dispersing magnesium perrhenate (0.5 wt%) into base oil to promote deposition of a protective layer during sliding over a wide temperature range.
papers.findings: The additive reduced the coefficient of friction by approximately 30.8% and decreased wear scar diameter by 28.5% in four-ball tests. At high temperature, a mixed protective layer (of Mg(ReO4)2 with natural oxides) formed that lowered friction compared to the base oil.
papers.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the soft, shear‐susceptible magnesium perrhenate compound deposits onto the worn surface, generating a protective lubricious film that minimizes direct asperity contact.

papers.title: Self-Lubricating Tribo-Catalytic Activity of 2D High Entropy Alloy Nanoflakes.
papers.system: 2D transition metal dichalcogenide high-entropy alloy nanoflakes, composition (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2, used as a spray-coated solid lubricant on steel
papers.approach: Synthesis and application of a 2D HEA structure that, under sliding conditions in ambient air (with residual ethanol), catalyzes tribochemical reactions.
papers.findings: The HEA nanoflakes demonstrated a low average coefficient of friction (~0.076) and extremely low wear rates (≈2.6 × 10⁻⁹ mm³/(N·m)) at high loads, with the formation of a tribolayer containing amorphous carbon and retained HEA fragments.
papers.mechanism: The high catalytic activity of the nanoflakes drives dissociation of entrapped ethanol, converting it to an amorphous carbon (a‑C) tribofilm. This in situ formed tribolayer provides low shear strength and continuous lubrication during friction.

papers.title: Reactive wear protection through strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces.
papers.system: TiNbZr-Ag alloy processed to impart self-adaptive in situ oxide nanocomposite formation during wear
papers.approach: Designing an alloy that reacts with environmental oxygen during sliding to form an in situ, ~400 nm thick amorphous–crystalline oxide layer containing Ag nanocrystals
papers.findings: Under air exposure during sliding, the alloy exhibited an ultra-low friction coefficient (~0.09) and significantly reduced wear rates (up to two orders of magnitude lower than TiNbZr alone) via formation of a protective surface layer.
papers.mechanism: The reactive wear protection mechanism entails the in situ formation of a strong, deformable oxide nanocomposite that mitigates adhesive and oxidative wear by continuously renewing the lubricious interface.

papers.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi₀.₅ High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Bulk AlCoCrFeNiTi₀.₅ high-entropy alloy produced by spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Processing HEA via SPS, enabling fine microstructure and taking advantage of protective oxide film formation at high temperatures
papers.findings: At elevated temperatures, the alloy showed increased wear resistance and a slight decrease in COF due to the generation of a protective oxide layer; microstructural stability was maintained during wear, supporting high-temperature use.
papers.mechanism: Wear resistance improves at high temperature as tribo-oxidation leads to formation of a stable, continuous oxide film which reduces metal-to-metal contact and abrasive wear.

established: Addition of certain solid lubricating additives (e.g., Mg(ReO4)2) can significantly reduce COF and wear by forming protective surface films over a wide temperature range.
Tribocatalytically active 2D high-entropy alloy nanoflakes can induce in situ formation of lubricious amorphous carbon tribofilms.
Alloy design that drives reactive wear protection (via controlled oxide nanocomposite formation) effectively minimizes wear.

approaches_tried.approach: Blending lubricating additives (such as Mg(ReO4)2) into a base oil to generate a protective layer during friction
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved 30% reduction in friction and substantial improvements in wear resistance at both low and high temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Employing 2D HEA nanoflakes that catalyze the in situ formation of an amorphous carbon tribolayer
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced remarkably low friction (COF ≈ 0.076) and extremely low wear rates, supporting self-lubrication in ambient air when residual solvent is present.

approaches_tried.approach: Reactive wear protection via alloying (e.g., adding Ag in TiNbZr-based alloys) to promote oxide nanocomposite formation
approaches_tried.outcome: Resulted in ultra-low friction (~0.09) and dramatically reduced wear rates by in situ generation of a protective, strong, and deformable tribolayer.

mechanisms: Formation of protective lubricious films via deposition of soft, shear-susceptible compounds (e.g., magnesium perrhenate).
Tribocatalytic activity of 2D nanoflakes that converts ambient or residual molecules (such as ethanol) into a lubricious amorphous carbon (a‑C) layer.
In situ reactive oxidation leading to the formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite that mitigates wear.
disagreements: The role of solvent chemistry: While 2D HEA nanoflakes show excellent performance in ethanol (through tribocatalytic conversion), similar tests in water failed, indicating that the availability and nature of the carbon source is critical.
There is some differing emphasis on whether friction reduction is solely due to the lubricious tribofilm or also significantly supported by microstructural strengthening via reactive wear protection.
open_questions: Can a single, alloy-integrated intervention provide both self-lubrication and reactive protection without reliance on external solvents?
What is the long-term stability of the tribolayer formed by tribocatalytic reactions under cyclic load and variable environmental conditions?
How do these mechanisms scale when transitioning from laboratory-scale tests (e.g., ball-on-disk) to full-scale moving components in practical machines?
opportunities: Combining tribocatalytic 2D HEA nanoflakes with alloy design strategies that favor reactive wear protection could synergistically improve lubrication across a broader temperature range.
Exploring alloy surface treatments that embed or generate catalysts for in situ formation of protective carbon or oxide films without relying on external lubricants.
Investigating the integration of catalysts that are effective in dry conditions to eliminate the dependency on solvents like ethanol, thereby broadening the applicability of self-lubricating HEAs.

directions.direction: Alloying with a reactive element (e.g., Ag) to enable in‐situ formation of an oxide nanocomposite tribolayer
directions.assessment: This approach targets the wear and friction issues by promoting a controlled reactive wear protection mechanism; the Ag dopant segregates during sliding to catalyze formation of a lubricious oxide nanocomposite. Prior evidence from TiNbZr–Ag systems supports its efficacy in reducing COF and wear, and the underlying physics of reactive oxidation is well established.

directions.direction: Surface coating with tribocatalytic 2D HEA nanoflakes
directions.assessment: Applying a thin layer of catalytically active 2D HEA nanoflakes can trigger in-situ tribochemical reactions that form a low-shear amorphous carbon (a‑C) tribofilm. This mechanism, supported by studies on (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2, directly lowers friction; however, it depends on the availability of a carbon source under ambient conditions.

directions.direction: Incorporation of a solid lubricating additive phase (magnesium perrhenate) within the HEA matrix
directions.assessment: Dispersing a small amount of magnesium perrhenate into the alloy can promote deposition of a soft, shear‐susceptible lubricious film during sliding, as demonstrated in oil-based tests. The mechanism is well understood and can be adapted to a solid alloy, though interfacial integration must be carefully controlled.

directions.direction: Laser surface alloying to embed a lubricious phase (MoS2) into the near‐surface region
directions.assessment: Using a laser treatment to create a surface layer enriched with MoS2 can form an in situ, self-replenishing solid lubricant during operation. This intervention is supported by evidence on MoS2-coated HEA systems but must consider potential decomposition at high temperatures.

candidates.hypothesis: Homogeneously dispersing 0.5–1 wt% pre-synthesized magnesium perrhenate (Mg(ReO4)2) particles within a bulk AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will, during sliding, facilitate the deposition of a lubricious film that reduces both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide temperature range.
candidates.intervention: Introduce 0.5–1 wt% magnesium perrhenate particles into the feedstock during alloy synthesis to achieve a uniform dispersion within the metallic matrix.

candidates.hypothesis: Laser surface alloying to embed approximately 5 wt% MoS2 into the top ~10 µm of an AlCoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy substrate will produce a self-replenishing, lubricious surface layer that reduces friction and wear across a broad temperature range.
candidates.intervention: Apply a controlled laser surface alloying process to incorporate ~5 wt% MoS2 into the top ~10 µm of the HEA, thereby achieving a homogeneous surface layer enriched with the lubricious phase.
